rows.question: How does LoRA avoid additional inference latency?
rows.answer:
[LoRA p.4]
When deployed in production, we can explicitly compute and store W = W0 + BA and perform inference as usual. Note that both W0 and BA are in Rd⇥k. When we need to switch to another downstream task, we can recover W0 by subtracting BA and then adding a different B0A0, a quick operation with very little memory overhead. Critically, this is done without introducing any additional latency.

rows.question: Why are positional encodings needed in the Transformer?
rows.answer:
[Positional Encoding]
Since our model contains no recurrence and no convolution, in order for the model to make use of the
order of the sequence, we must inject some information about the relative or absolute position of the
tokens in the sequence. To this end, we add "positional encodings" to the input embeddings at the
bottoms of the encoder and decoder stacks. The positional encodings have the same dimension dmodel
as the embeddings, so that the two can be summed. There are many choices of positional encodings,

The answer is that positional encodings are needed in the Transformer to make use of the order of the sequence.
rows.reference: Because the Transformer has neither recurrence nor convolution, positional encodings inject information about the relative or absolute positions of tokens.

rows.question: What type of positional encoding did the paper use?
rows.answer:
[Attention is all you need  p.6]
The paper used a sinusoidal positional encoding, which is defined as:

PE(pos,2i) = sin(pos/100002i/dmodel)
PE(pos,2i+1) = cos(pos/100002i/dmodel)

where pos is the position and i is the dimension.
rows.reference: It used sine and cosine functions of different frequencies, with one sinusoid corresponding to each dimension.
